def: The four weeks before Christmas, a season of hopeful waiting. It begins the Church year.
Hebrew for "praise the Lord." Sung before the Gospel, except during Lent.
The table at the front of the church where the Eucharist is celebrated.
Hebrew for "yes, so be it." Saying it means you agree with and believe the prayer.
The twelve men Jesus chose to lead his Church. Bishops today are their successors.
The first sacrament. Through water and the Holy Spirit, we are freed from sin, become children of God and members of the Church.
A successor of the apostles who leads a diocese (a local Church made up of many parishes).
In OCIA, someone already baptized in another Christian church who is preparing to be received into full communion.
A summary of what the Church teaches. The Catechism of the Catholic Church is the official one.
Someone who teaches the faith, such as the leaders of your OCIA group.
In OCIA, someone who is not yet baptized and is preparing for baptism.
The cup that holds the wine that becomes the Blood of Christ at Mass.
Receiving the Body and Blood of Christ in the Eucharist. Also means our unity with God and one another.
The sacrament that seals us with the gift of the Holy Spirit and strengthens us to live as witnesses.
The moment in the Eucharistic Prayer when the bread and wine become the Body and Blood of Christ.
A statement of what Christians believe, such as the Apostles' Creed or the Nicene Creed.
An ordained minister who serves the Church: he can baptize, preach, read the Gospel at Mass and witness marriages.
A region of the Church led by a bishop, made up of many parishes.
Catechumens who have been chosen at the Rite of Election to receive the sacraments at Easter.
The sacrament of Jesus' Body and Blood, and the name for the Mass itself. From the Greek for "thanksgiving."
To bend the right knee to the floor as a sign of reverence toward Jesus in the tabernacle.
"Good news." Also the four books of Matthew, Mark, Luke and John about the life of Jesus.
God's free gift of his own life and help within us.
The third Person of the Trinity, who gives life to the Church and helps us live as Christians.
The talk after the Gospel at Mass, explaining the readings.
The round wafer of bread used at Mass, which becomes the Body of Christ.
The book of Scripture readings used at Mass.
The forty days before Easter, a season of prayer, fasting and giving to those in need.
The Church's public worship, especially the Mass and the sacraments.
The celebration of the Eucharist, the central act of Catholic worship.
The time after Easter when the newly baptized reflect on the sacraments they received. From the Greek for "leading into the mysteries."
A newly baptized person. From the Greek for "new plant."
Order of Christian Initiation of Adults, the way adults join the Catholic Church. Formerly called RCIA.
Your local Catholic community and church, led by a pastor.
Jesus' passion, death, resurrection and ascension, by which he saved us.
Turning away from sin. Also the prayer or action the priest gives you in confession.
The Bishop of Rome, successor of St. Peter and visible head of the Church.
An ordained minister who celebrates Mass, hears confessions and cares for a parish.
The belief that Jesus is truly present, Body, Blood, soul and divinity, in the Eucharist.
The sacrament of confession, in which God forgives our sins through the priest.
A prayer with beads that meditates on the life of Jesus and Mary through repeated prayers.
A visible sign, given by Christ, through which God gives us his grace. There are seven.
A person in heaven. The Church officially recognizes some as models of holy living.
Prayers for healing and strength for the elect on the 3rd, 4th and 5th Sundays of Lent.
A Catholic who accompanies you through OCIA and stands with you at the rites.
The box, often gold, where consecrated Hosts are kept. A candle burns beside it.
One God in three Persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
A celebration the evening before a feast, like the Easter Vigil on Holy Saturday night.
